bib.title: Evaluating ChatGPT's Information Extraction Capabilities: An Assessment of Performance, Explainability, Calibration, and Faithfulness

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Evaluating ChatGPT's Information Extraction Capabilities: An Assessment of Performance, Explainability, Calibration, and Faithfulness", Bo Li, Gexiang Fang, Yang Yang, Quansen Wang, Wei Ye, Wen Zhao, Shikun Zhang (Peking University, Boston University). arXiv:2304.11633v1 [cs.CL], 23 Apr 2023. Preprint. The PDF names no venue. Code and data: github.com/pkuserc/ChatGPT_for_IE.

COVERAGE: All 18 pages read, 76,592 of 76,592 chars. That covers the body, tables 1-11 and the appendix (A.1 datasets, A.2 SOTA methods, A.3 input example). References were skimmed only. There is no limitations section and no results appendix beyond the dataset counts. Offsets are character offsets in the extraction, approximate. Appendix starts at about 68544.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- ChatGPT, given a label set, is far below supervised BERT/RoBERTa/SOTA on most IE tasks. It beats them only on entity typing.
  number: BBN ET 85.6 vs SOTA 82.2; CoNLL NER 67.2 vs 94.6; TACRED RC 20.3 vs 75.6; ACE05-E ED 17.1 vs 75.8; ACE05-E EE 17.0|7.3 vs 74.7|56.8
  setup: ChatGPT (official API, March 2023-era), whole test sets, Micro-F1. Prompt is task description + label set + input + output-format instruction. Conversation cleared after each response. Baselines are supervised and cited or re-run.
  quote: "ChatGPT's performance is not comparable to that of baseline models and SOTA methods in most cases." Table 2 row: "CoNLL2003 92.8 92.4 94.6 (Wang et al., 2021) 67.2"
  where: sec 4.2, Table 2, about 20-23k

- Performance drops as task complexity rises: ET is good, NER/RC are middling, and RE/ED/EAE/EE are poor.
  number: ET 85.6 / 73.4; ACE05-R RE 40.5|4.5; SciERC RE 25.9|5.5
  setup: as above
  quote: "ChatGPT's performance varies based on the complexity of the task, and it performs well on straightforward tasks."
  where: sec 4.2

- Judged without a label set (OpenIE), ChatGPT's outputs are often reasonable. The gap against the label-set accuracy is large, and the label set itself seems to hurt.
  number: Standard vs OpenIE accuracy: BBN 86.8% vs 97.2%; CoNLL 69.0% vs 93.3%; SemEval 43.3% vs 84.3%; ACE05-E ED 12.4% vs 42.6%; EAE 17.3% vs 65.3%; EE 4.9% vs 28.8%; RE 14.9% vs 23.9%
  setup: about 200 random samples per dataset. OpenIE correctness is a majority vote of 3 domain experts on whether the prediction is "reasonable", not a match to ground truth. Standard is exact match to the gold label.
  quote: "more than 84% of the predictions are considered reasonable by the domain experts in ET, NER, and RC tasks." Also: "some labels are not easy to understand, thereby negatively impact the performance."
  where: sec 4.3, Table 3, sec 4.2

- Top-k answers act as a candidate generator. Recall rises sharply from top-1 to top-5.
  number: BBN 85.6 -> 92.7 -> 94.9 (+9.3); SemEval2010 42.5 -> 62.1 -> 76.0 (+33.5); the text gives top-3 gain on SemEval as 19.6%
  setup: whole test set, asked for top3 and top5 labels from the given label set. Only 2 datasets are reported ("other datasets show similar observation").
  quote: "BBN 85.6% 92.7% 94.9% (+9.3%)  SemEval2010 42.5% 62.1% 76.0% (+33.5%)"
  where: sec 4.4, Table 5

- Self-reported verbal confidence is overconfident and badly calibrated, especially on harder tasks. ChatGPT's ECE is much worse than BERT/RoBERTa except on ET.
  number: ECE ChatGPT vs BERT: BBN 0.026 vs 0.012; CoNLL 0.204 vs 0.052; SemEval 0.460 vs 0.023; ACE05-R 0.745 vs 0.020; ED 0.656 vs 0.161; EAE 0.699 vs 0.154; EE 0.699 vs 0.211
  setup: ChatGPT is asked to output an integer confidence from 1 to 100 (0-100 in the appendix prompt) with each prediction. ECE uses 50 equal-width bins. Whole test set.
  quote: "ChatGPT shows much poorer calibration compared to BERT-based methods" and "it displays overconfidence in both correct and incorrect predictions."
  where: sec 5.2, Tables 6-7, footnote 8

- The confidence gap between correct and incorrect predictions is small in some tasks, and on EAE the incorrect-prediction confidence is nearly as high as the correct one.
  number: Table 6 EAE ChatGPT correct 0.956 / incorrect 0.910. BBN 0.888 / 0.828. ACE05-R 0.760 / 0.764.
  quote: "ACE05-E(EAE) 0.762 0.785 0.956 0.525 0.555 0.910"
  where: Table 6. Note: the authors also write "we note a significant confidence gap between correct and incorrect predictions", which fits only some rows. This is my reading of the table, not an authors' claim.

- ChatGPT's self-judged explanation quality is about 100%, so self-check is inflated against human-check. Human-check is high on simple tasks and low on EE and EAE.
  number: Standard setting self-check 100% on all datasets; human-check BBN 99.2, ACE05-R 90.0, ED 96.3, EAE 74.1, EE 47.1. OpenIE human-check EE 78.0 (self 94.0).
  setup: only samples with correct Standard-IE predictions are evaluated. About 200 samples per dataset, 3 domain experts. The reason and the "if_reasonable" self-rating come in the same output JSON.
  quote: "ChatGPT achieves nearly a 100% reasonable score among almost all datasets. This suggests that ChatGPT is very confident in its ability to provide reasonable explanations."
  where: sec 5.1, Table 4

- Explanations are faithful to the input text.
  number: over 95% faithful in nearly all datasets; the lowest is ACE05-R Standard at 90.0%, the rest 93.8-100%.
  setup: correct predictions only, manual annotation of whether the reason is fictitious.
  quote: "with over 95% of samples considered faithful in nearly all datasets under different settings."
  where: sec 5.3, Table 8

- Why this paper's verdict differs from earlier positive IE reports (Wei et al. 2023; Gao et al. 2023): it scored whole test sets with one concise unified prompt, while prior work used small random subsets and domain-specific or label-description-heavy prompts.
  number: none
  quote: "prior studies reported on a very small set of test samples drawn at random, which may have substantial variance."
  where: sec 4.2

- Evaluation design: 15 keys across 4 dimensions (performance, explainability, calibration, faithfulness). 10 keys come from ChatGPT's own JSON output and 5 are manual.
  number: 7 tasks, 14 datasets, "nearly 3,000" manually annotated samples
  quote: "we randomly select nearly 3,000 samples in total for our analysis."
  where: sec 4.1, Table 1. Per-dataset annotated counts are in Table 9 (e.g. SemEval 400, ACE05-R 66, EE 552). Table 9 labels BBN as "ED", which looks like a typo for ET.

LIMITS
- Zero-shot, single prompt, no few-shot demonstrations, no CoT variation, and no prompt-sensitivity test. The authors concede that the prompt choice may explain the contrasts with prior work.
- Only gpt-3.5-era "ChatGPT" (Mar-Apr 2023) is tested. The model version is not stated, and it has dated heavily. Current models would score differently.
- Human judgement is "reasonable" by 3 experts with no reported inter-annotator agreement. OpenIE "correctness" does not require matching the ground truth, so it is not comparable with Standard-IE accuracy.
- The explainability and faithfulness subsets are conditioned on correct predictions. They exclude failures.
- Explanations and verbal confidence come in the same output as the answer, which may influence the answer. This is not tested.
- The OpenIE/explainability samples are small (about 200 per dataset; ACE05-R only 66 annotated).
- Calibration uses verbalised confidence, not token probabilities. Other models are compared on softmax probabilities, so the confidence measures are not like for like.
- Table 5 shows only 2 datasets. Results on a 14-dataset study are partly asserted.
- No limitations section.

BUILDS ON: Guo et al. 2017 (calibration/ECE, overconfidence); Maynez et al. 2020, He et al. 2023 (faithfulness); Wei et al. 2022b (CoT); Ouyang et al. 2022 (instruction/RLHF); Brown et al. 2020; Rajani et al. 2019, Zini and Awad 2023 (explainability); Qin et al. 2023, Bang et al. 2023 (ChatGPT evaluations); Wei et al. 2023, Gao et al. 2023 (contrasting ChatGPT IE reports). The task and SOTA datasets include Zuo et al. 2022, Wang et al. 2021, Ye et al. 2022, Hsu et al. 2022, Lin et al. 2020.

CODE: Table 11 (appendix A.3, about 70k) shows the evaluation prompt structure: Task Description, Pre-defined Label Set, Input and Task Requirement. The output is a JSON list of dictionaries with nine keys: "trigger", "word_index", "event_type", "top3_event_type", "top5_event_type", "confidence", "if_context_dependent", "reason", "if_reasonable". It ends with: "Note that your answer should only contain the json string and nothing else." The confidence key is "an integer ranging from 0 to 100".

FIGURES: There are no figures. The tables carry the results: Table 1 (the 15 keys), Table 2 (performance), Table 3 (Standard vs OpenIE), Table 4 (explainability), Table 5 (top-k), Table 6 (confidence), Table 7 (ECE), Table 8 (faithfulness). I did not run the figures script.

PROBLEMS: The extraction is clean, apart from ligature glyphs ("ﬁ", "ﬂ"), which I normalized in the quotes to ASCII. Quotes are otherwise verbatim except for line breaks and hyphenation joins. The PDF gives no page numbers per claim, so I used section and table references. I found no embedded instructions. The paper is a preprint with no stated venue. If the target note cites it as an EMNLP/ACL paper, that is not supported by the PDF.
